prize_parts.citation: For incorporating firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, changing how exporting, reallocation and the gains from trade are analysed.

statement.case_for: I keep B021 first after reading the openings. Firm heterogeneity and selection moved trade analysis from industries to firms. Melitz (2003) and the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple work on exporting versus FDI explain who exports, why liberalisation raises aggregate productivity through reallocation, and why gains from trade have a within-industry channel that earlier models missed. The predictions have been tested against firm-level data in many countries for more than twenty years. The framework is now the standard starting point for empirical and quantitative trade work. Attribution is among the cleaner on the shortlist: Melitz's model is the pivotal contribution and Helpman supplied the broader theory and extensions. Trade has not been recognised since Krugman in 2008, and this is a distinct step from that prize because it concerns selection among firms rather than increasing returns and love of variety. I also value that the framework connects theory to micro data and so meets the same standard of credible evidence that I apply to empirical fields.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is credit. The empirical firm-level facts (Bernard and Jensen) and the closely related Eaton-Kortum framework sit outside this ballot entry, so a Helpman-Melitz prize could be read as crediting the theory and under-crediting the empirical groundwork. The welfare conclusions also depend on functional-form assumptions, notably Pareto productivity distributions. Krugman's 2008 prize may lead some members to treat this as a continuation of the same line. Helpman's other candidacy (B044) creates a risk of splitting support and credit. Finally, B001 has much broader support and arguably greater policy reach, and a more convergent set of proposed laureates.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B021 first. He sees Melitz (2003) as the central contribution, with Helpman's work on exporting and FDI completing the core, and Redding as important but more derivative. He flags credit sharing with Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum.
responses.response: I agree on the two-name core and on treating Redding as a successor on quantitative and spatial extensions. I do not think the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum issue can be waved away. The empirical regularities on exporter premia came first, and Eaton-Kortum is a parallel structural route to gains from trade. I would argue that the committee can still credit the selection model that organised those facts and made welfare predictions from them. That is a narrower claim than crediting all firm-level trade research, and the citation should be worded that way.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B001 first, with Calvo, Taylor and Woodford as the defensible trio, and ranks B006 second, calling the political-economics case mature and arguably overdue.
responses.response: I accept that B001 is the strongest alternative to my preferred option. Nominal rigidities clearly deserve recognition, and the trio is the most plausible three-person cut. My hesitation is that Calvo pricing, Taylor contracts and the rule, and Woodford's synthesis are three different types of contribution, while Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets have claims that a trio leaves out. I also take the post-2021 inflation debate seriously as a test of the framework. On B006 I would be more cautious than Krusell. Even if the field is mature, much of the constitutional-effects evidence relies on cross-country variation, and the 2024 institutions prize makes the marginal contribution harder to judge. That is why I rank it sixth. I note his disclosed IIES proximity to Persson. I do not treat it as bearing on the merits.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B001 first, with Calvo, Taylor and Woodford. He acknowledges that choosing three from a large group is contestable and that Gertler's overlap with the 2022 prize and with B002 may matter.
responses.response: I share his reading of the attribution problem, and I think it is the main reason to hesitate about B001. The fact that nearly every member proposes the same three names is useful evidence that the originators are widely identified. It does not remove the exclusions of Gali, Gertler and the Christiano-Eichenbaum group. I would not count that agreement as scientific merit, but I do count it as a sign that the credit assignment is less arbitrary than it first looks. I disagree with his ranking of B021 fourth because he treats Redding as a follower rather than a co-originator. That reasoning supports the two-name award I propose.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B002 first. He says the Kiyotaki-Moore collateral mechanism is foundational and tractable, that the attribution is clean, and that its overlap with the 2022 prize may reduce novelty.
responses.response: I agree that Kiyotaki and Moore is the cleanest attribution among the macro candidates, and I rank it third. I remain unsure about two things. The mechanism's influence is stronger on the theory side than in direct identification of collateral channels. The 2022 recognition of banking and financial crises also partly covers the policy motivation. If the committee prefers a macro-finance award, I would support the two-person version without Gertler and Gilchrist, but I still find B021's combination of theory and firm-level testing more persuasive.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat Helpman-Melitz as a distinct advance from Krugman's 2008 prize or as the same lineage.
How much weight to give the empirical firm-level pioneers (Bernard, Jensen) and Eaton-Kortum, who are outside this ballot entry.
Whether the welfare and gains-from-trade results are robust enough to functional-form assumptions to support a citation centred on gains from trade.
How to weigh B001's much broader opening support and convergent laureate proposals against its diffuse attribution and the unresolved post-2021 inflation debate.
My assessments rely on general knowledge and the ballot descriptions, not on independent verification of the literature.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for B021. I am an empirical labour economist at Uppsala with no stated connection to Helpman or Melitz. I overlapped institutionally with the Stockholm/IIES environment from 2010 to 2017, but the profile records no co-authorship with Persson or other B006 candidates. My field is close to B010 and B047, which are not part of my preferred configuration.
